_comment: The Map of the Future. Part A is the raw thematic list, uncurated. Part B is what survives a filter of: one person, home hardware, near-zero capital, and not already a bloodbath. No dates anywhere, deliberately. It is a map, not a schedule. Owner ruling 2026-09-04: the corpus provenance line and the candidate list are off the page.

part_a.title: Everything that could be built
part_a.note: Uncurated. Includes things needing capital, hardware, a lab or a team, because the ask was complete rather than pre-filtered.

themes.name: AI agents and automation
items: Agent permission, sandboxing and audit-trail tooling
Context compression and token-cost reduction middleware
AI browsers and AI-native search replacements
themes.built: Three of these exist here: AmoebiX dispatches the question across models, AegisBox is the room the code runs in, AgentMesh is how they find each other.

themes.name: Verification, trust, epistemics
themes.built: AxiomTEA lives here and is finished. AxiomVerify and SynapseGraph point the same instinct at arguments and at citations.
items: Prediction-tracking databases: who predicted what, when, and were they right
Automated replication labs for scientific claims
Deception and hidden-cheating detectors for model outputs
Evidence verification engines cross-checking claims against data

themes.name: Energy
items: Orbital solar arrays and space-based power beaming
Enhanced geothermal colocated with data centres
Grid load balancing and virtual power plants
themes.built: GridPulse moves heavy compute to the cheap hours. FlowGrid works out whether the battery pays for itself.

themes.name: Longevity and biotech
items: Multi-omic aging clocks and biological age tracking
Personalized nutrition and continuous biomarker tracking
themes.built: EpiGuide designs the guides. It cannot see the whole genome yet, and says so on every run.

themes.name: Robotics and physical automation
themes.built: Kinematix, and it is a teaching simulator rather than anything that drives a robot.

themes.name: Transportation
themes.built: OmniFleet, once somebody put a clock in it.

themes.name: Space
items: Lunar and Mars in-situ resource utilization
Satellite constellations and orbital data centres

themes.name: Materials and nanotech
items: Molecular-scale synthesis platforms: print any material
Carbon nanotube manufacturing at macro scale
themes.built: CrystalGen screens the candidates before anyone books lab time.

themes.name: Food and agriculture
themes.built: AquaNutrient watches the reservoir. There is no hardware in it.

themes.built: close to an AI fluency curriculum already written
items: AI personal tutors and adaptive curricula

themes.name: Economics, finance, work
items: Compute financialization: GPUs as tradable assets
Workforce displacement mapping and retraining engines

items: AI governance, compliance and audit fabric
Model release policy and evaluation frameworks

themes.name: Consciousness and AI welfare
items: Mechanistic interpretability tooling, including distress-signature detection in model internals
AI welfare and alignment evaluation frameworks

part_b.title: What one person could actually build
filter: One person, home hardware. Nothing here needs serious local compute; anything model-heavy calls a hosted API.
No lab equipment, no manufacturing, no regulatory approval pathway, no physical supply chain.
Not already saturated by well-funded competitors.
A narrow, identifiable buyer. Not everyone. A specific small population with this exact problem now.

top_pick.name: Citation and reference integrity checker
top_pick.why_now: The problem I hit twice in the conversation that produced this list. AI research assistants fabricate specific-sounding citations, episode numbers, guest names, dates and URLs that do not survive a check against the real source. My own 900 KB research corpus is full of it: invented episode numbers, claims attributed to episodes that may not say what is claimed.
top_pick.what_it_does: Paste in a document. It extracts every citation-shaped claim and checks it against real public metadata, podcast feeds, video APIs, publisher sites, then flags each one CONFIRMED, MISMATCHED where the source exists but does not say that, or NOT FOUND where the source does not appear to exist at all.
top_pick.why_it_clears: Near-zero capital on free public APIs. Narrow enough not to compete with AxiomTEA, which does physics rather than citations, or with general fact-checkers, which do political truth rather than source existence. The buyer is concrete and growing: anyone using AI for research who has been burned by exactly this. And the test corpus already exists, for free, in my own files.
